title: An interpretation-independent formulation of the measurement problem
abstract: In this paper, we do not try to solve the measurement problem, but rather to properly formulate it. One of the reasons why it still lacks a precise, agreed definition is that the problem may take very different aspects depending on the interpretation of quantum mechanics embraced. Inspired by the methodology of theory-independent results like Bell's theorem, we propose to identify the common root of the puzzle in an interpretation-independent way i.e. as a property of the empirical statistics only, before deriving its philosophical consequences. The key observation is that quantum matter can not be described by a Kolmogorovian probabilistic theory. Arguing that the Kolmogorov axioms of probability theory are the postulates of epistemic uncertainty leads us to reformulate the measurement problem as the impossibility to build an ontology independent of epistemology for quantum matter. Said differently, there exists no God's-eye view on quantum systems. Although it is meaningless to solve the measurement problem as defined in this way, insofar as it is a feature of the universe's statistics, such a formulation may on the other hand bring side benefits. In particular, we argue that it allows to: (i) shed a new light on the variety of interpretations; (ii) propose a fundamental reason why quantum mechanics and general relativity are so incompatible, not relying on purely mathematical or technical arguments; (iii) guide the quest for quantum gravity.
summary: This paper reframes the measurement problem not as a physical puzzle to be solved, but as a fundamental statistical inconsistency: quantum mechanics violates the axioms of classical probability theory. By establishing this non-Kolmogorovian nature of quantum statistics, the authors propose a framework that has profound implications for quantum gravity and the nature of objective reality.
main_problem: The paper addresses the quantum measurement problem by seeking an interpretation-independent formulation, rather than attempting a direct solution.
main_result: The core finding is that quantum matter cannot be described by a Kolmogorovian probabilistic theory, suggesting the problem lies in the incompatibility between quantum statistics and classical probability axioms.
method: The methodology involves analyzing the empirical statistics of quantum measurements, comparing them against the axioms of classical probability (Kolmogorov theory), and drawing parallels with theory-independent theorems like Bell's theorem.
model_or_system: The focus is on the abstract mathematical properties of quantum mechanical predictions and their empirical statistics, rather than a specific physical Hamiltonian or system.
key_observables: Violation of the Law of Total Probability (LTP), violation of Bell-type inequalities, and the non-Kolmogorovian nature of quantum interference statistics.
important_parameters: None specified; the focus is on fundamental axioms and statistical properties.
main_assumptions: The authors assume that the conflict arises because the standard axioms of probability (Kolmogorov) are insufficient to describe quantum reality, leading to the conclusion that no 'God's-eye view' exists.
paper_structure: The paper moves from reviewing the limitations of existing interpretations to establishing the non-Kolmogorovian nature of quantum statistics through statistical diagnostics, and finally discussing the philosophical implications for quantum gravity and the nature of reality.
why_interesting: It provides a fundamental, statistical framework for understanding the measurement problem that transcends specific interpretations, which is crucial for developing a unified theory of quantum gravity.
